gradingRubric.A: Primary or verified: peer-reviewed study, government statistics, vendor's own pricing page, our own CI output. Page opened on the access date.
gradingRubric.B: Two independent secondary sources agree, or one reputable aggregate with a stated sample size.
gradingRubric.C: One secondary source, or company-reported figures repeated by a single outlet, or sources that conflict.
gradingRubric.D: Model-generated, unsourced or contradicted. Never a model input or a headline.

claims.claim: Concurrent training does not significantly reduce maximal-strength gains versus strength training alone
claims.source: Schumann M. et al. Compatibility of Concurrent Aerobic and Strength Training for Skeletal Muscle Size and Function. Sports Medicine 52 (2022). 43 studies, 1,090 participants

claims.claim: Concurrent training does not significantly reduce muscle hypertrophy
claims.source: Schumann et al., Sports Medicine 2022

claims.claim: Concurrent training does significantly attenuate explosive-strength (power) gains
claims.source: Schumann et al., Sports Medicine 2022

claims.claim: Explosive-strength attenuation was larger when aerobic and strength work were in the same session than when separated by at least 3 h; running vs cycling, frequency, training status and age did not moderate the effect
claims.source: Schumann et al., Sports Medicine 2022 (moderator analysis: same session p = 0.043; >= 3 h separation p > 0.05)

claims.claim: Recovery between concurrent sessions matters: strength gains were lower with 0 h than 6 h or 24 h, and VO2peak improved most with 24 h. 'Daily training without a recovery period between sessions (C-0h) and, to a lesser extent, training twice a day (C-6h), is not optimal'
claims.unit: hours (best of 0 / 6 / 24 h tested); n = 58 amateur rugby players, 7 weeks
claims.source: Robineau J. et al. Specific Training Effects of Concurrent Aerobic and Strength Exercises Depend on Recovery Duration. J Strength Cond Res 30(3), 2016

claims.claim: A graded program built on the 10% weekly-progression rule did not reduce running injuries versus a standard program (20.8% vs 20.3%, n = 532 novice runners, RCT)
claims.source: Buist I. et al. No Effect of a Graded Training Program on the Number of Running-Related Injuries in Novice Runners. Am J Sports Med 36(1), 2008

claims.claim: The ACWR 'sweet spot' (0.8-1.3) was not protective: 27.5% of all injuries (83% in pentathletes) occurred inside it
claims.unit: % of injuries inside the sweet spot
claims.source: Sedeaud A. et al. Does an Optimal Relationship Between Injury Risk and Workload Represented by the 'Sweet Spot' Really Exist? Frontiers in Physiology 2020

claims.claim: Older meta-analysis reported smaller strength, hypertrophy and power gains with concurrent training than strength training alone
claims.source: Wilson J.M. et al. Concurrent training: a meta-analysis. J Strength Cond Res 26(8), 2012 - summarised by Stronger by Science; primary abstract not opened (publisher paywall, Europe PMC rate-limited)
